citizenship.heroTitle: Turkish Citizenship by Real Estate Investment
citizenship.heroSubtitle: HADARA provides trusted, end-to-end guidance for international investors seeking Turkish citizenship through property investment.
citizenship.introText: Türkiye grants citizenship to foreign investors who buy real estate worth at least $400,000 and keep it for a minimum of three years. Your spouse and children under 18 are included in the same application, there is no requirement to live in Türkiye, and you can keep your current nationality.
citizenship.introText2: HADARA guides you through every stage — choosing an eligible property from our projects, the valuation, payment and title deed, then the citizenship file prepared with our legal partners — so the process stays clear and on schedule.
citizenship.requirementsSubtitle: The main conditions a real estate investment must meet to qualify for Turkish citizenship.

requirements.title: Minimum value of $400,000
requirements.desc: The property must be worth at least USD 400,000, or the equivalent in another foreign currency. The amount can be reached with a single property or with several properties together.

requirements.title: Official valuation report
requirements.desc: An appraisal company licensed by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) values the property, and the value in its report must meet the threshold.

requirements.title: Payment in foreign currency
requirements.desc: The price is paid by bank transfer in foreign currency, converted at a Turkish bank against a Foreign Currency Purchase Certificate (DAB) that proves the investment.

requirements.title: Three-year holding commitment
requirements.desc: An annotation is added to the title deed stating that the property will not be sold for at least three years.

requirements.title: Certificate of Conformity
requirements.desc: Once the purchase is registered, the Land Registry issues a Certificate of Conformity confirming that the investment meets the program's conditions.

requirements.title: Off-plan homes qualify
requirements.desc: Homes under construction are also eligible through a notarised promise-to-sell agreement carrying the same three-year commitment.

citizenship.rulesNote: The figures on this page reflect the rules in force at the time of writing and may change. Our team confirms the current requirements before any purchase.
citizenship.stepsSubtitle: Most steps can be handled through a power of attorney, so a short visit to Istanbul is usually enough.

steps.title: Free consultation
steps.desc: We discuss your goals, budget and family members, and shortlist eligible projects and units.

steps.title: Property selection and reservation
steps.desc: Visit in person or by live video, choose your unit and secure it with a reservation agreement.

steps.title: Tax number and bank account
steps.desc: We help you obtain a Turkish tax number and open a local bank account, both needed for the purchase.

steps.title: Valuation and payment
steps.desc: The licensed valuation report is prepared and the price is transferred in foreign currency, with the DAB certificate issued by the bank.

steps.title: Title deed
steps.desc: Ownership is registered at the Land Registry with the three-year annotation — or, for off-plan homes, the notarised promise-to-sell agreement is signed.

steps.title: Certificate of Conformity
steps.desc: The Land Registry reviews the file and issues the Certificate of Conformity for the citizenship application.

steps.title: Residence permit and application
steps.desc: You and your family obtain residence permits, and the citizenship application is submitted with the full set of documents.

steps.title: Approval, ID card and passport
steps.desc: After the authorities' review, the citizenship decision is issued and you apply for your Turkish ID cards and passports.

citizenship.stepsNote: From the title deed to the decision, the process usually takes a few months, depending on the authorities' review.

faq.heroSubtitle: Answers to the questions we hear most often about HADARA, investing in Turkish real estate, and Turkish citizenship by investment.

items.a: HADARA Real Estate is a boutique real estate development and investment company founded in 2014, headquartered in Beylikdüzü, Istanbul. We design, build and deliver residential and mixed-use developments and private villas across Beylikdüzü and Büyükçekmece.

items.q: What types of projects does HADARA develop?
items.a: Our portfolio spans master-planned residential communities, mixed-use developments combining residences, offices and retail, and bespoke luxury villas — each built with quality construction and long-term value in mind.
All of our current developments are located on Istanbul's European side, in the fast-growing districts of Beylikdüzü, Büyükçekmece, Avcılar and Şişli.

items.q: How can I get in touch with HADARA's team?
items.a: You can reach us through the Contact page, by phone at +90 531 930 92 14, or by email at info@byhadara.com. Our team is available every day, 09:00–18:00 (Istanbul time).

items.q: Why invest in real estate in Istanbul?
items.a: Istanbul combines a growing economy, expanding infrastructure and strong rental demand, making it one of the most attractive real estate markets connecting Europe and Asia. Districts like Beylikdüzü and Büyükçekmece are among the fastest-growing on the European side.

items.q: Can foreign nationals buy property in Turkey?
items.a: Yes. Citizens of most countries can freely purchase residential and commercial property in Turkey, subject to standard title deed procedures. Our team guides international buyers through every step.
HADARA offers flexible installment payment plans on select projects, in addition to standard cash purchase, making it easier for both residents and investors to secure a unit.

items.q: What costs should I budget for beyond the purchase price?
items.a: Typical additional costs include the title deed transfer fee, the appraisal report, and standard administrative charges. Our team will walk you through the full cost breakdown for any project you're interested in.

items.q: Is buying property in Turkey a good rental investment?
items.a: Istanbul's strong tourism and population growth support healthy rental demand, particularly in mixed-use and centrally located developments such as Lotus İstanbul.

categories.title: Turkish Citizenship by Real Estate Purchase

items.q: How can I obtain Turkish citizenship by buying property?
items.a: Turkey's citizenship-by-investment program allows foreign nationals who purchase qualifying real estate above a minimum value, and hold it for at least three years, to apply for Turkish citizenship.

items.q: What is the minimum investment amount required?
items.a: Under the current program rules, the minimum qualifying real estate investment is $400,000 USD (or equivalent). HADARA's team can confirm which of our projects meet this threshold.

items.q: Does citizenship extend to my family?
items.a: Yes. Your spouse and children under 18 are included in the same citizenship application at no additional investment.

items.q: How long does the process take?
items.a: After the property purchase and valuation report are completed, the citizenship application typically takes a few months to be reviewed and approved by the Turkish authorities.

items.q: Can I keep my current nationality?
items.a: Yes. Turkey permits dual citizenship for most nationalities, so you are not required to give up your original citizenship.

items.q: Do I need to live in Turkey to qualify?
items.a: No. There is no residency requirement before or after approval — you can maintain the property as an investment without relocating.

citizenship-property.title: Citizenship by buying property from $400,000
citizenship-property.text: A foreigner can apply for Turkish citizenship after buying one or more properties worth at least US$400,000 or its equivalent, with a 3-year no-sale annotation on the title deed. It is also possible for a property under construction through a promise-to-sell contract signed before a notary, provided the full amount is paid upfront.

residence-property.title: Residence permit through property
residence-property.text: Owning a home in Turkey allows you to apply for a short-term residence permit. The official list of documents of the Presidency of Migration Management requires the home to be worth at least US$200,000 or its equivalent in Turkish lira at the time of purchase, and to be used as your home, not rented out.

residence-closed-areas.title: Neighbourhoods closed to new residence permits
residence-closed-areas.text: The Presidency of Migration Management closes some neighbourhoods and districts to new residence permit applications by foreigners, based on population density, and updates these lists from time to time. If a residence permit is your goal, check the address before you buy.

valuation-report.title: Valuation report required in sales to foreigners
valuation-report.text: Since 4 March 2019, the Land Registry has required a valuation report showing the market value of the property in every sale where a foreigner is the buyer or the seller.

currency-certificate.title: Converting foreign currency through a Turkish bank
currency-certificate.text: When a foreigner buys property, the price is converted from foreign currency into Turkish lira through a bank in Turkey, and the currency purchase certificate issued by the bank (Döviz Alım Belgesi) is presented to the Land Registry.

title-deed-fee.title: Title deed fee of 4%
title-deed-fee.text: Under Fees Law No. 492, the title transfer fee (Tapu Harcı) is 2% for the buyer and 2% for the seller, a total of 4% of the declared sale value.

property-tax.title: Annual property tax
property-tax.text: Property owners pay an annual property tax (Emlak Vergisi) to the municipality. Homes whose value exceeds a threshold set every year also pay the valuable housing tax (Değerli Konut Vergisi).

rent-increase.title: Limit on residential rent increases
rent-increase.text: When a residential lease is renewed, the yearly increase may not exceed the 12-month average change in the consumer price index (TÜFE), under Article 344 of the Turkish Code of Obligations No. 6098.

citizenship-amount-certificate.title: Citizenship amount certificate now valid for 6 months
citizenship-amount-certificate.summary: The Land Registry amended its Circular No. 2024/4: the purchase amount for citizenship is now confirmed by an Amount Determination Certificate (Tutar Tespit Belgesi) issued by the valuation company GEDAŞ after an electronic comparison.
citizenship-amount-certificate.before: The valuation report was valid for 3 months from its date of issue.
citizenship-amount-certificate.after: Certificates issued after 9 December 2024 are valid for 6 months, and the value written on the certificate is used directly in the title deed transaction.
citizenship-amount-certificate.affects: Foreigners buying property to obtain Turkish citizenship.
citizenship-amount-certificate.help: We keep track of the certificate's validity with you so that the title transfer is completed in time.

property-tax-cap-2026.title: A limit on the 2026 property tax increase
property-tax-cap-2026.summary: Law No. 7566, published in the Official Gazette, limits how much the value used for the annual property tax can rise in 2026.
property-tax-cap-2026.after: The 2026 tax value of buildings and land may not exceed twice their 2025 tax value.
property-tax-cap-2026.affects: Everyone who owns property in Turkey and pays the annual property tax.
property-tax-cap-2026.help: We explain the expected yearly taxes and fees of a property before you buy.

title-deed-declared-price.title: Higher penalty for declaring a lower price at the land registry
title-deed-declared-price.summary: Law No. 7566 increased the penalty when a sale is registered at the land registry at a price below the real price or below the property tax value.
title-deed-declared-price.before: The tax-loss penalty on the unpaid fee difference was 25%.
title-deed-declared-price.after: The penalty now equals the full unpaid fee difference (one-fold).
title-deed-declared-price.affects: Buyers and sellers in any property sale.
title-deed-declared-price.help: We always advise registering the real price at the land registry and accompany you through the title transfer.

valuable-housing-tax-2026.title: 2026 threshold for the valuable housing tax
valuable-housing-tax-2026.summary: The Revenue Administration updated the value from which the valuable housing tax (Değerli Konut Vergisi) applies.
valuable-housing-tax-2026.affects: Owners of homes whose tax value exceeds this threshold.
valuable-housing-tax-2026.help: We tell you whether the property you choose may be subject to this tax.

savings-finance-foreigners.title: No purchases by foreigners with savings finance loans
savings-finance-foreigners.summary: The Land Registry announced that foreigners cannot acquire property with loans from savings finance companies (Tasarruf Finansman Şirketleri).
savings-finance-foreigners.after: A property purchase by a foreigner cannot be financed through these companies.
savings-finance-foreigners.affects: Foreigners planning to finance a purchase through a savings finance company.
savings-finance-foreigners.help: We help you plan a suitable payment method before you buy.

secure-payment-system.title: Secure payment system mandatory in property sales from December 2026
secure-payment-system.summary: The Ministry of Trade amended the Real Estate Trade Regulation and set 1 December 2026 as the start of mandatory use of the secure payment system in property sales.
secure-payment-system.after: From 1 December 2026, the secure payment system becomes mandatory in property sales. It connects the Land Registry's systems with banks so that the payment and the title transfer are completed together.
secure-payment-system.affects: Buyers and sellers of property in Turkey.
secure-payment-system.help: We will walk you through the payment and title transfer steps under the new system when you buy.

rent-regulation-board-bill.title: Bill to create a Rent Regulation Board
rent-regulation-board-bill.summary: A bill amending the Mass Housing Law and the Turkish Code of Obligations was submitted to the Turkish parliament, proposing a Rent Regulation Board (Kira Düzenleme Kurulu).
rent-regulation-board-bill.after: The bill proposes that the board set the conditions for benefiting from social housing and the maximum rents by province and region. It is still being discussed in committee and is not law yet.
rent-regulation-board-bill.affects: Tenants and landlords, if the bill is passed.
rent-regulation-board-bill.help: We follow the bill and will update this page if it is passed and published in the Official Gazette.

gross-vs-net-area.title: Gross vs Net Area and What 2+1 Means in Turkish Listings
gross-vs-net-area.excerpt: Learn how to read gross (brüt) and net areas and the 2+1 layout code, with real examples from HADARA's projects.
body: Open any property listing in Istanbul and you will quickly meet two words that confuse many first-time buyers: gross and net. Add a code such as 2+1, and a brochure can start to look like a puzzle. This guide explains what these terms mean and how to use them when you compare homes, so that the numbers on the page become clear before you ever step into a sales office.
## Gross and net: what is the difference?

Gross area, called brüt in Turkish, is the larger figure. It measures the apartment together with its walls and usually a share of the building's common parts. Net area, called net, is the usable floor space inside the apartment: the part you actually walk on, furnish and live in. Because gross includes more, it is always the bigger number, and brochures and price lists very often quote it first.

Neither figure is wrong. They simply answer different questions. Gross tells you how the unit is measured and sold on paper, while net tells you how much room you will really have at home. When you compare two apartments, always compare gross with gross and net with net, and never a gross figure from one project with a net figure from another. Otherwise a smaller home can look larger than it is.
## What does 2+1 mean?

In Turkish listings the first number counts the rooms, usually used as bedrooms, and the second number counts the living rooms, called salon. A 2+1 therefore has two bedrooms and one living room, with the kitchen and bathrooms counted separately. A 3+1 has three bedrooms and a living room, and a 1+1 has one bedroom and a living room. Keep in mind that the code says nothing about size: two 2+1 apartments can differ clearly in area, so always read the square metres printed beside the layout.
## Real examples from our projects

Cadde Ispartakule offers 2+1 apartments of 106.30 – 108.56 m² gross, with 89.66 – 91.92 m² net, and 3+1 apartments of 132.83 – 150.61 m² gross, with 116.19 – 133.97 m² net. In every case the net figure is the smaller one, exactly as you should expect. Lotus Şişli lists a 1+1 with 57.56 m² gross and 43.41 m² net, and a 2+1 with 83.75 m² gross and 63.16 m² net. Its catalog also quotes a third figure, the saleable gross area (satışa esas brüt), of 75.97 m² and 110.53 m² for those two types. It is a useful reminder to ask exactly which area the price is based on.

Villas follow the same logic, level by level. Marmara Haven Villa gives gross and net for each floor: the basement has 138.62 m² gross and 105.40 m² net, the ground floor 223.37 m² gross and 108.60 m² net, the first floor 143.19 m² gross and 126.21 m² net, and the rooftop level 103.66 m² gross and 82.82 m² net. The gap between the two figures is not the same on every level, which shows why one overall number never tells the whole story. Lotus Yaşam, by comparison, shows gross ranges, for example 100 – 109 m² for its 2+1 apartments, so it is worth asking for the net figure of the exact unit you like.
## Questions to ask before you decide

Ask which area the price is based on, whether the net area is shown on the floor plan, and which parts are counted inside the gross figure. Ask to see the floor plan of the exact unit, and compare each room with the way you plan to live: where the sofa, the dining table and the beds will go. A plan on paper is easier to judge once you can see the real rooms and the show apartment, and a video tour is a practical way to start. Please note that the figures above come from the project catalogs and may be updated by the developers.

HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, is happy to go through floor plans with you and explain every number. Contact us or book a private video tour to shortlist the homes that suit you, then visit Istanbul to see them in person.

real-estate-in-turkey.title: Investing in Turkish Real Estate: A Practical Guide for Foreigners
real-estate-in-turkey.excerpt: Why and how foreigners invest in Istanbul property: types of homes, new launch or ready to move in, what to check, and choosing a trusted partner.
body: Istanbul sits where Europe meets Asia, and for many foreign buyers it is the natural first step into Turkish real estate. Citizens of most countries can buy residential and commercial property in Turkey, subject to the standard title deed procedures, and the market offers everything from compact city apartments to sea-view villas. Yet a good purchase is never only about the property. It starts with a clear reason for buying, continues with careful checks, and ends with a title deed in your name. This guide sets out the main decisions in order.
## Why foreigners buy in Istanbul

Buyers come with different goals, and naming yours first makes every later choice easier. Some want a home for their family or a second home for long stays. Others look for a property they can rent out, or for a combination of a home and a commercial unit. Many are also interested in what ownership can bring: under the current rules, real estate worth at least USD 400,000, held for at least three years, can lead to Turkish citizenship for the buyer, the spouse and children under 18, while a home worth at least USD 200,000 in Istanbul can support a renewable residence permit. These conditions are per current law and may change. Rental income and future value depend on the location, the unit and the market, so treat any investment as a long-term decision rather than a guaranteed return.
## Types of property to consider

Apartments in residential complexes are the most common choice, usually described by layout codes such as 2+1 or 3+1 and sold with access to shared facilities. Villas offer more space and privacy: Lotus Manzara Güzelce has 6+2 detached villas, Lotus Manzara Beylikdüzü has 5+2 detached and twin villas, and Marmara Haven Villa is a single private residence with panoramic sea views. Central mixed-use projects add other options, such as the home offices and street-front shops of Lotus Şişli or the street-level shops of Cadde Ispartakule. When you compare sizes, remember that Turkish listings quote both gross and net areas, a difference we explain in a separate article.
## New launch or ready to move in?

A new launch or a project under construction lets you choose from the widest range of units, often early in the sales process, and selected projects offer flexible installment payment plans. Lotus Yaşam in Beylikdüzü is scheduled for delivery in late 2028, Diamond Marin in late 2027, and Lotus Şişli is currently under construction. The trade-off is time: you wait for delivery, so the developer's track record, the delivery date written in the contract and the payment schedule deserve close attention. Off-plan homes can also qualify for citizenship through a notarised promise-to-sell agreement.

A completed project removes much of the uncertainty. You can walk through the actual apartment, see the view from the balcony, get to know the complex as it really is, and move in or rent it out without waiting. Lotus Koru 2, Cadde Ispartakule and Lotus Yalı are completed with residences available, as are the villa communities of Lotus Manzara Güzelce and Lotus Manzara Beylikdüzü, and Marmara Haven Villa. The choice between the two paths usually comes down to your timeline and how you prefer to pay.
## What to check before you buy

Location comes first: transport links such as the Metrobüs, the metro and the E-5 and TEM highways, and the distance to schools, hospitals, the sea and the airport. Then the building itself: the type of title deed, the building permit and, for completed buildings, the occupancy permit known as iskan, compliance with the 2018 Turkish Earthquake Code, and whether there is any mortgage or lien on the title. Ask which area the price is based on, and whether the address is open to residence registrations for foreigners. Finally, budget for the costs beyond the price, such as the title deed fee of 4% of the declared value and the report of a licensed valuation company.

A trusted local partner turns this checklist into a clear process. HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, helps you define your goal, shortlist the projects that match it, read floor plans and documents, obtain a tax number and open a bank account, and follows your file until the title deed is registered. We present only what the project documents confirm, and we tell you plainly when a unit does not meet a requirement such as the citizenship threshold.

The easiest way to start is a conversation. Contact our team or book a free private video tour: your advisor will show you the show apartment, the scale model and the project on site, and answer your questions on payment plans, delivery and citizenship. The tour helps you choose before you travel, and when you are ready to buy, we arrange your visit to Istanbul and accompany you at every step.

citizenship-by-real-estate.title: How to Get Turkish Citizenship by Buying Property: A Buyer's Guide
citizenship-by-real-estate.excerpt: A practical guide to Turkish citizenship through property: what to buy, the steps, the documents and which family members are included.
body: Many international buyers first look at Istanbul because of the home itself, then discover that the same purchase can lead to Turkish citizenship for the whole family. Turkey grants citizenship to foreign investors who buy real estate worth at least $400,000 and keep it for at least three years. This guide follows the buyer's side of that journey: what to look for in a property, the order of the steps, the documents to prepare and how your family fits into the application. The legal conditions themselves are covered in a separate article on the citizenship-by-investment law.
## Choosing a property that qualifies

Start with the purpose. A home bought for citizenship still has to work as a home or as an investment, so think about location, size and how you plan to use it, then check eligibility. The property must be worth at least USD 400,000 or the equivalent in another foreign currency, and the amount can be reached with one property or with several properties together. Eligibility belongs to the unit, not to the project as a whole: in the same building, a larger apartment may reach the threshold while a smaller one does not. Homes under construction can also qualify, so an off-plan unit is not ruled out.

Ask for written confirmation before you commit. For some projects HADARA publishes a Verified Project Card with details confirmed by our team. For Marmara Haven Villa, for example, that card lists the property as eligible for citizenship. For other projects, our advisors check each unit you shortlist against the current rules, so you never rely on a brochure alone.
## The journey, step by step

The process begins with a free consultation, where we discuss your goals, budget and family members and shortlist eligible projects and units. A private video tour is a practical next step: with one of our advisors you can see the show apartment, the model and the site itself, and ask every question before you travel. The purchase itself is completed on a visit to Istanbul, where you see your chosen home in person. Around this time you will also need a Turkish tax number and a local bank account, and our team helps you obtain both.

Next comes the formal part. A licensed valuation report is prepared, the price is transferred in foreign currency and the bank issues a DAB certificate. Ownership is then registered at the Land Registry with an annotation that the property will not be sold for three years, or, for an off-plan home, a notarised promise-to-sell agreement is signed. The Land Registry reviews the file and issues a Certificate of Conformity. You and your family then obtain residence permits, the citizenship application is submitted, and after the authorities' review the decision is issued and you apply for Turkish ID cards and passports. Many of these formalities can be handled through a power of attorney, so a short visit to Istanbul is usually enough. From the title deed to the decision, the process usually takes a few months.
## Documents and your family

One purchase covers the family. Your spouse and children under 18 are included in the same application, with no additional investment. There is no requirement to live in Turkey before or after approval, and dual citizenship is permitted for most nationalities, so you can usually keep your current passport. Preparing documents early saves time. You will need valid passports for yourself, your spouse and your children, birth certificates showing the parents' names, a marriage certificate if applicable, and recent biometric photographs. The property file adds the title deed or the notarised promise-to-sell agreement, the valuation report, the DAB certificate, the Certificate of Conformity and the residence permits. Documents issued abroad need an apostille, or consular legalisation, and a sworn Turkish translation. Our team prepares the file with you and checks every document before submission.
## Planning your budget

Besides the property price, plan for the title deed fee, which is 4% of the declared property value and is paid at registration, the valuation report, sworn translations and notary costs, official fees for residence permits, the application and passports for each family member, and the fees of the lawyers who prepare and follow the citizenship file. We prepare a detailed estimate for your case. The amounts and conditions in this article reflect the current law and may change, so our team confirms the rules in force before any purchase.

HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, is happy to walk you through eligible homes and the full citizenship process. Contact us or book a private video tour to build your shortlist, then visit Istanbul to see the homes in person and take the next step with confidence.

about-turkey.title: Living and Investing in Turkey: A Country Between Two Continents
about-turkey.excerpt: Turkey's geography, culture and connections, and why so many foreigners choose it as a place to live and invest.
body: Turkey is one of the few countries in the world that belongs to two continents at once. Its larger part lies in Anatolia, in Asia, while a smaller part, Thrace, lies in Europe. For anyone thinking of moving abroad or buying property outside their home country, this position explains a great deal: the country's history, its culture, its climate and the way it connects people and markets. This introduction gives you a broad picture of Turkey before you look at a specific city, district or home.
## A land between Europe and Asia

Turkey is surrounded by water on three sides. The Black Sea lies to the north, the Aegean to the west and the Mediterranean to the south, while the Sea of Marmara sits inside the country, linked to the Black Sea by the Bosphorus and to the Aegean by the Dardanelles. Between these coasts stretch high plateaus, mountain ranges, lakes and fertile plains. The result is a country of strong contrasts: green forests along the Black Sea, warm beaches in the south and west, and wide open landscapes in the interior, with clear seasons and a different climate in each region.
## Culture and everyday life

Over the centuries, Anatolia and Thrace have been home to many civilisations, and their traces are still visible in ancient sites, Byzantine churches and Ottoman mosques, palaces and bazaars. Turkish culture gives great importance to family and hospitality, and newcomers often notice how quickly neighbours, shopkeepers and colleagues make them feel welcome. Food is a central part of daily life, from long family breakfasts to tea shared at any time of day. At the same time, the large cities offer a fully modern way of life, with shopping centres, international schools, private hospitals, cafés and cultural venues, so tradition and modern living sit side by side.
## Connected to the world

Turkey's location makes it a natural crossroads. Istanbul Airport, on the European side of Istanbul, is one of the main air hubs linking Europe, the Middle East, Asia and Africa, and many cities in these regions can be reached with a direct flight. Within the country, motorways, high-speed rail lines and domestic flights connect the major cities, while Istanbul itself relies on a growing network of metro lines, the Metrobüs and main roads such as the E-5 and the TEM. For families who travel often, or who keep business ties in more than one region, this connectivity is one of the strongest practical reasons to choose Turkey.
## Why foreigners choose Turkey

People from many countries choose Turkey for a mix of reasons: a comfortable lifestyle, a culture that feels familiar to many newcomers from the region, varied landscapes within easy reach, and a property market open to foreign buyers. New residential communities are often planned as complete living environments, with landscaped gardens, fitness centres, pools, indoor car parks and 24/7 security. Buyers can choose between city apartments, homes close to the sea, villas with private gardens and home offices in business districts, depending on whether they want a family home, a second residence or an investment.

Property can also open the door to residence and citizenship. Under the current rules, a foreign investor who buys real estate worth at least $400,000 and keeps it for at least three years can apply for Turkish citizenship, together with a spouse and children under 18, without having to live in Turkey and while keeping their current nationality. For buyers who are not seeking citizenship, owning a home can also support a renewable residence permit. The conditions are per current law and may change, so each case should be checked before you buy.

For most international buyers, the journey begins in Istanbul, the country's largest city and its main gateway to the world. It brings together the sea, green districts, business centres and a wide range of new projects, which is why we cover it in a separate guide. Before choosing a district, it helps to decide what matters most to you: being close to the sea, to nature, to work or to good transport links.

HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, can help you turn this broad picture into a clear shortlist. Contact us or book a private video tour to see suitable homes and ask your questions, then visit Istanbul to view them in person before you decide.

about-istanbul.title: Living in Istanbul: Beylikdüzü, Büyükçekmece, Avcılar and Şişli
about-istanbul.excerpt: A guide to Istanbul's two sides and to four of its districts, from sea and nature in the west to city life in Şişli.
body: Istanbul is often described as one city, but anyone who spends time here soon discovers that it is many cities in one. Each district has its own rhythm, its own landscape and its own daily routine. Choosing where to live in Istanbul is therefore just as important as choosing the home itself. This guide explains how the city is organised and what four districts on its European side offer: Beylikdüzü, Büyükçekmece, Avcılar and Şişli.
## The European side and the Asian side

The Bosphorus runs through the middle of Istanbul and divides it between Europe and Asia, linking the Black Sea in the north with the Sea of Marmara in the south. Bridges, road tunnels and rail lines under the strait connect the two sides, and each side has its own international airport: Istanbul Airport on the European side and Sabiha Gökçen Airport on the Asian side. The European side holds the historic peninsula with Sultanahmet, as well as Taksim and the city's main business districts, while the Asian side is known for its residential neighbourhoods along the water.

West of the city centre, the European side stretches along the Marmara coast. This is where the E-5 highway, also known as the D-100, and the Metrobüs line run, with the TEM motorway further north and the Northern Marmara Motorway beyond it. Along these corridors, districts such as Beylikdüzü, Büyükçekmece and Avcılar have grown into complete places to live, with marinas, beaches, parks, shopping centres and hospitals, while Şişli remains part of the busy heart of the city.
## Beylikdüzü: marinas, parks and everyday comfort

Beylikdüzü combines the coast with a well-organised urban life. West Istanbul Marina and the Gürpınar coastline lie by the sea, while Beylikdüzü Yaşam Vadisi offers a long green valley for walks and sport. MarmaraPark and Torium malls, several private hospitals and the E-5 with the Metrobüs cover daily needs. From Diamond Marin, for example, West Istanbul Marina and Yaşam Vadisi are 5 minutes away and the Metrobüs 10 minutes. The district suits many lifestyles: boutique apartments near the marina, villas with sea-view terraces such as Lotus Manzara Beylikdüzü, homes beside a large park in Lotus Koru 2, and the new Lotus Yaşam community.
## Büyükçekmece: between the sea and nature

Further west, Büyükçekmece is for those who want calm, green surroundings with the sea close by. Güzelce Marina, the Güzelce coastline, Mimar Sinan Yacht Harbour and Kıyı İstanbul Marina give the district a strong seaside character, and Büyükçekmece State Hospital and the E-5 are within reach. Lotus Manzara Güzelce sets its villas between woodland and the Marmara Sea, Lotus Yalı turns its blocks towards the sea and gives most of its site to gardens, and from Marmara Haven Villa the Marmara Sea swimming coast is 5 minutes away and the E-5 3 minutes. Many buyers choose this district for a quieter, more spacious way of life.
## Avcılar and Şişli: connections and city life

In Avcılar, the Ispartakule area is described as one of Istanbul's most sought-after growth districts. Cadde Ispartakule looks out over the sea, a lake and the route of the planned Kanal Istanbul, and sits close to the TEM and Northern Marmara motorways and Istanbul Airport. Akbatı Mall, Mall of Istanbul, Bahçeşehir Pond and Başakşehir City Hospital are among the places nearby, which makes the area practical for families who drive and travel often.

Şişli is a different world: a central business district full of offices, hospitals, hotels and shops. Lotus Şişli, on Piyalepaşa Boulevard, is 100 m from Memorial Şişli Hospital, 540 m from the Darülaceze–Perpa Metrobüs stop and 1 km from Çağlayan Metro, with Cevahir Mall 1.5 km, Nişantaşı 2 km and Taksim 2.9 km away. Its home offices, apartments and penthouses suit buyers who want to live, work or invest in the middle of the city.

The right district depends on how you want to live: by the sea, close to nature, near the motorways or in the centre of the city. life-in-turkey.title: Life in Turkey for Foreign Families: Settling In Istanbul
life-in-turkey.excerpt: A practical guide for foreign families settling in Istanbul: choosing a district, life in a residential complex, schools, services and paperwork.
body: Moving to a new country is a family decision before it is a property decision. Before you compare floor plans, you want to know how an ordinary week will feel: the school run, the weekly shopping, a walk by the sea, a visit to the doctor, a friendly face in the lift. Istanbul is a vast city that has long welcomed people from many countries, and most foreign families find that daily life settles into a comfortable rhythm once a few practical choices are made. This guide walks through those choices in the order most families meet them.
## Choosing your part of Istanbul

Istanbul is less one city than a collection of very different districts, so the first question is how you want to live. On the European side, Beylikdüzü and Büyükçekmece look towards the Marmara Sea, with marinas, coastal walks and green valleys such as Beylikdüzü Yaşam Vadisi, and they are linked to the rest of the city by the E-5 highway and the Metrobüs. The Ispartakule area of Avcılar sits close to the TEM and Northern Marmara motorways and the road to Istanbul Airport. Şişli, by contrast, is central Istanbul: metro and Metrobüs stops, large hospitals, business centres and the shops of Nişantaşı are all close at hand.

A good way to decide is to sketch your family's week. Where will the adults work, and how will they get there? How far is the school you are considering? Do you prefer to hear the sea, to be surrounded by trees, or to have the city on your doorstep? Families who answer these questions first usually narrow their search to one or two districts very quickly, and the right home becomes much easier to recognise.
## Life inside a residential complex

Many families in Istanbul live in a site, the Turkish word for a gated residential complex with shared facilities. In the residential projects we offer, these usually include separate swimming pools for men and women, a fitness centre, an indoor car park, 24/7 security with camera surveillance, cleaning of the shared interiors, landscaped gardens and a backup generator. Some go further: Lotus Yaşam adds a children's playground, a sports court and a walking and jogging track, while Lotus Yalı and Cadde Ispartakule include a sauna and a Turkish bath. Villa communities such as Lotus Manzara Güzelce and Lotus Manzara Beylikdüzü offer a private garden and a covered garage for two cars with every villa instead.

For a family, these shared spaces shape everyday life as much as the apartment itself. Children play in the gardens within sight of home, parents meet neighbours at the gym or by the pool, and security at the entrance brings peace of mind when you travel. The shared facilities are run by the complex management and funded by a monthly maintenance fee known as aidat, so it is wise to ask what the fee covers and how it is managed before you choose. Turkish neighbours are generally warm and welcoming, and a simple greeting in the lift or a glass of tea offered on the terrace is often the start of a real friendship.
## Schools, health care and daily services

Istanbul has state schools, private Turkish schools and international schools teaching in other languages, and the choice of school often decides the district, so visit or contact schools early and ask about places, languages and transport. Each project page on our site lists the hospitals nearby, for example Medicana International Istanbul and Medilife Beylikdüzü in the western districts, Büyükçekmece State Hospital, Başakşehir City Hospital near Ispartakule, and Memorial Şişli Hospital beside Lotus Şişli. For shopping, malls such as MarmaraPark, Torium, Akbatı and Mall of Istanbul sit alongside the weekly neighbourhood markets, where many families buy their fruit and vegetables.
## Paperwork and residence

A few administrative steps make daily life simpler, such as obtaining a Turkish tax number and opening a local bank account. Buying a home can also entitle you to a renewable residence permit: under the current rules the property must be worth at least USD 200,000 in Istanbul, and your spouse and children under 18 can obtain permits too. Some neighbourhoods are closed to new residence registrations for foreigners, so the address should be checked before you buy. Families with a larger budget sometimes consider Turkish citizenship through property instead. These conditions are per current law and may change, so our team confirms them before any purchase.

Settling in is easier with someone who already knows the city. HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, can help you compare districts and complexes around your family's routine. Contact us or book a private video tour: your advisor will show you the homes and introduce the neighbourhood, from transport and schools to shopping and the distance to the sea and the airport. buying-property-and-tapu.title: How to Buy Property in Turkey and Register the Title Deed (Tapu)
buying-property-and-tapu.excerpt: A step-by-step guide to buying property in Turkey, from choosing and reserving a home to the title deed appointment and receiving your Tapu.
body: Buying a home in Turkey becomes a clear, well-organised process once you know the order of the steps. Citizens of most countries can buy property in Turkey, and the purchase follows a set sequence: choose the property, reserve it, prepare a few documents, complete the valuation and the payment, and register the sale at the Land Registry Office, where the title deed, known as the Tapu, is issued in your name. This guide explains each stage, so you know what to expect from the first viewing to the day you receive your Tapu.
## Choosing the home and reserving it

Everything starts with the right property. Compare the locations, layouts, gross and net areas and payment options of each project, and see the homes in person on a visit to Istanbul, or first through a private video tour with our advisors. Once you have decided, a reservation agreement secures the unit for you and records the agreed price, the payment method and the next steps. Payment can be made in cash, and installment plans are offered on select projects. A home that is still under construction is usually sold through a notarised promise-to-sell agreement, and the title deed transfer follows at a later stage.
## Documents and checks before you pay

Before the payment, two practical items are needed: a Turkish tax number and an account at a local bank. Both are simple to obtain, and our team helps you with them. You will also need a valid passport, and any document issued abroad, such as a power of attorney, usually needs an apostille or consular legalisation and a sworn Turkish translation. If you cannot stay in Istanbul for every step, many of them can be handled through a power of attorney, so a short visit is usually enough.

This is also the time to check the property itself. Ask about the type of title deed, the building permit, the occupancy permit (İskan) for a completed building, and whether there is any mortgage or lien on the property. If you plan to apply for a residence permit, confirm that the neighbourhood is open to new residence registrations for foreigners, because some areas are closed to them. For Marmara Haven Villa, these points are shown on a Verified Project Card confirmed by the HADARA team, and copies of the documents can be requested.
## Valuation, payment and the title deed appointment

Before the transfer, a foreign buyer needs an official valuation report prepared by an appraisal company licensed by the Capital Markets Board (SPK). The report confirms the value of the property and becomes part of the file at the Land Registry. The price is then paid by bank transfer, following the schedule in your agreement. If you are buying for Turkish citizenship, the payment is made in foreign currency and converted at a Turkish bank against a Foreign Currency Purchase Certificate (DAB). Keep every receipt and bank document, as they show where the money came from and how it was paid.

On the day of the appointment, the seller and the buyer, or their representatives holding a power of attorney, attend the Land Registry Office (Tapu Müdürlüğü). If you do not speak Turkish, a sworn translator is present to explain the documents before you sign. The title deed fee is paid at registration, and the costs of a purchase are explained in our separate article on taxes and fees. Once the documents are signed, the property is registered in your name and the new Tapu is issued. For a citizenship purchase, an annotation is added stating that the property will not be sold for at least three years.
## After you receive your Tapu

Keep the original title deed in a safe place, together with copies of the valuation report and the payment documents. Next, transfer the electricity, water and natural gas subscriptions to your name, and make sure the property is recorded at the local municipality for the annual property tax. In a residential compound, you will also start paying the monthly building management fee, known as aidat. If you bought for citizenship, the Land Registry then issues the Certificate of Conformity, which opens the way to the residence permit and the application itself. Please note that these procedures follow current law and may change, so they should be confirmed for each purchase.

HADARA, your real estate partner in Istanbul, coordinates each of these steps with you, from the first shortlist to the day you receive your Tapu. Contact us to talk about your plans, or book a private video tour to start choosing your home before your visit to Istanbul.

taxes-and-tapu-fees.title: Property Taxes and Tapu Fees in Turkey: What Buyers Should Budget
taxes-and-tapu-fees.excerpt: Beyond the price: the 4% title deed fee, valuation, translations, annual property tax and running costs to plan for when buying in Turkey.
body: The price of a home is the largest part of your budget, but it is not the only one. Buying property in Turkey also involves a title deed fee, a few document and service costs, and running costs once you become the owner. None of them is unusual, yet a buyer who knows them in advance can compare projects fairly and avoid surprises on the day of the title deed appointment. This guide groups these costs into three families: the fee paid at registration, the other costs of the purchase, and the costs of owning the home.
## The title deed fee (Tapu fee)

The most significant one-off cost is the title deed fee, paid at the Land Registry Office when the sale is registered. It is 4% of the declared property value. On the project pages of HADARA's website, prices include VAT and the 4% title deed registration fee is not included, so add it to your budget as a separate line. Before the appointment, make sure your agreement states clearly what the price covers and how the fee will be handled.

The declared value matters because the fee is calculated on it, and it should reflect the real price you pay. A value set too low in order to reduce the fee can cause problems later, for example when you sell the property, or when its value has to be proven for a citizenship or residence permit application.
## Other costs of the purchase

A foreign buyer needs an official valuation report from a licensed appraisal company, and its fee is part of the purchase budget. Documents usually bring their own costs as well: sworn translations of your passport and other papers, notary fees for a power of attorney, an apostille or consular legalisation for documents issued abroad, and a sworn translator at the title deed appointment if you do not speak Turkish. Your bank may also charge for international transfers and currency conversion, and some buyers choose to work with a lawyer, whose fees should be agreed in advance.

If you are buying for Turkish citizenship, add the official fees for residence permits, the application and passports for each family member, as well as the fees of the lawyers who prepare and follow the citizenship file. These items depend on the size of your family and on the official fee schedules in force, which is why we prepare an estimate for each case.
## The costs of owning the home

Once the property is registered in your name, an annual property tax is paid to the local municipality. Its rate is set by law and depends on the property and the municipality, so ask for the current figure for the home you choose. In a residential compound, a monthly building management fee, known as aidat, covers shared services such as security, cleaning, gardens and pools; it differs from one project to another, and it is worth asking about it before you buy. You will also open subscriptions for electricity, water, natural gas and internet, which may involve connection costs or deposits. In addition, Turkey has a compulsory earthquake insurance for homes, known as DASK, which is renewed every year.
## Planning your budget with confidence

The simplest approach is to ask for a written cost estimate for the exact unit you are considering, covering the title deed fee, the valuation report, translation and notary costs, and the expected running costs. If you plan to rent the home out or sell it one day, ask a qualified accountant about the taxes on rental income and on the sale. Please remember that taxes, fees and rates are set by current law and may change, so they should be confirmed again for each purchase before you sign.

real-estate-valuation.title: Property Valuation Reports in Turkey: What Buyers Should Know
real-estate-valuation.excerpt: What a property valuation report is, who prepares it, what it checks and why it matters for buyers and for Turkish citizenship.
body: When you buy a home in Istanbul, the price you agree with the seller is only one side of the story. The other side is an independent opinion of what the property is actually worth, written down in a valuation report. For many foreign buyers this report is a formal step in the purchase, and for anyone applying for Turkish citizenship through real estate it is one of the key documents in the file. This guide explains what the report is, who prepares it, what it looks at and how it protects you.
## What a valuation report is and who prepares it

A valuation report, called gayrimenkul değerleme raporu in Turkish, is a written assessment of a property's market value on a given date. It is prepared by an appraisal company licensed by the Capital Markets Board of Turkey, known as SPK. A qualified appraiser visits the property, checks its records and compares it with similar properties, then sets out the value and the reasoning behind it. Because the appraiser works independently of both the buyer and the seller, the report gives an objective reference point rather than a sales figure.
## What the appraiser looks at

The first questions are about place. The appraiser considers the district and the street, access to main roads and public transport, the services nearby and the character of the surroundings. In a residential complex, the building and its shared facilities also count: the condition of the blocks, the gardens, the car park, the security and the social amenities that residents use every day.

The report then turns to the unit itself: its gross and net area, its layout such as 2+1 or 3+1, the floor, the view and the orientation, the quality of construction and finishes, and the age and condition of the building. The appraiser compares these features with recent sales of similar homes in the same area and checks the official records, such as the title deed details and the building's permits. For a home that is still under construction, the assessment is based on the project documents and plans, since the finished building cannot yet be inspected.
## Why it matters for Turkish citizenship

Under the citizenship by investment program, the property must be worth at least USD 400,000, or the equivalent in another foreign currency, and it is the value in the licensed valuation report that has to meet this threshold, not only the price written in the contract. The amount can be reached with one property or with several together. The report then joins the other documents of the file: the title deed, or a notarised promise-to-sell agreement for a home under construction, the bank's Foreign Currency Purchase Certificate (DAB) and the Certificate of Conformity issued by the Land Registry. These conditions follow current law and may change, so our team confirms the requirements in force before any purchase.
## How the report protects you as a buyer

Even if citizenship is not your goal, the valuation report is valuable protection. It lets you compare the asking price with an independent assessment, which helps you avoid paying more than a property is worth and gives you a clear basis for discussing any difference. It also leaves an official record of the property's value at the time of purchase, a useful document later if you decide to resell, seek financing or simply review your investment.

A few practical points help. Make sure the report describes the exact unit you are buying, with the same block, floor and unit number as the title deed or the contract. Check which area it uses, gross or net, so that you compare like with like. Ask what the value is based on if it differs noticeably from the price. And include the cost of the report in your budget, next to the title deed fee of 4% of the declared value, translations and notary fees.

citizenship-investment-laws.title: Turkish Citizenship by Investment: The Legal Conditions Explained
citizenship-investment-laws.excerpt: What Turkish law requires for citizenship by investment: minimum value, valuation report, foreign currency payment, three-year hold and other routes.
body: Turkish citizenship by investment is not a special visa product but a set of conditions written into regulations issued under Turkish citizenship law. These rules define which investments qualify, how their value is measured and proven, and what the investor commits to. Understanding them before you choose a property helps you avoid a purchase that looks right on paper but does not meet the program's requirements. This article explains each condition of the real estate route as it applies today, and then looks at the other investment routes the program accepts.
## The minimum value and how it is measured

The central condition is value. The property must be worth at least USD 400,000, or the equivalent in another foreign currency, and the threshold can be met with a single property or with several properties together, which gives buyers some flexibility in how they structure the investment. What counts, however, is not only the price agreed with the seller. An appraisal company licensed by the Capital Markets Board, known in Turkey as SPK, values the property, and the value stated in its official valuation report must meet the threshold. This is why the valuation report is part of the citizenship file, and why it is wise to check before signing that the expected valuation supports the amount you plan to invest.
## Payment in foreign currency

The law also sets how the money arrives. The price is paid by bank transfer in foreign currency, which is converted at a Turkish bank against a Foreign Currency Purchase Certificate, called DAB. This certificate proves that the investment was made in the required way. A payment that does not follow this route may not provide the proof the application needs, so the order of payment and paperwork matters as much as the amount itself. It is therefore worth agreeing with the seller and your bank, before any transfer, on how the payment will be made and documented.
## The three-year commitment and the Certificate of Conformity

An investor who buys for citizenship commits to keeping the property: an annotation is added to the title deed stating that it will not be sold for at least three years. In return, the same investment covers the family, and the spouse and children under 18 are included in the application without any additional investment. Because the annotation stays on the title deed for the whole period, a citizenship purchase is best planned as a medium-term commitment rather than a quick trade.

Once the purchase is registered, the Land Registry issues a Certificate of Conformity confirming that the investment meets the program's conditions. This certificate is the link between the property and the citizenship file. Homes under construction are also eligible: in that case the buyer signs a notarised promise-to-sell agreement that carries the same three-year commitment, so off-plan projects can qualify just as completed ones do.
## Other routes the program accepts

Real estate is the most popular route, but the regulations recognise other investments: a bank deposit of $500,000 kept in a Turkish bank for at least three years, Turkish government bonds of $500,000 held for at least three years, and $500,000 in shares of real estate or venture capital investment funds held for at least three years. A fixed capital investment of $500,000 in a business, confirmed by the Ministry of Industry and Technology, is another option, as is creating jobs for at least 50 people, confirmed by the Ministry of Labour. HADARA specialises in the real estate route; for the others, we refer you to trusted partners. Each of these routes has its own conditions and paperwork, and for the financial routes the three-year period applies as well.

The figures in this article reflect the rules in force at the time of writing and may change, because the government can update these regulations. This article is general information, not legal advice, and our team confirms the current requirements before any purchase.

real-estate-market-trends.title: Istanbul Real Estate Trends: What Buyers Look for Today
real-estate-market-trends.excerpt: How shared facilities, earthquake-resistant buildings, western districts, off-plan homes and home offices shape what buyers choose in Istanbul.
body: Istanbul's housing market is large and varied, and it keeps changing with the way people live and work. Rather than figures or forecasts, this article looks at the qualities that local and international buyers ask about most often today, and at how they appear in real projects across the city. Knowing them helps you judge a home not only by its price, but by how well it will suit your life in the years ahead.
## Complete communities with shared facilities

More and more buyers prefer a home inside a residential complex rather than a standalone building on a busy street. Families in particular value what a well-run complex offers within its own grounds: swimming pools, often separate for men and women, a fitness centre, landscaped gardens and playgrounds, an indoor car park, round-the-clock security with cameras, cleaning of the common areas and a backup generator. Lotus Yaşam in Beylikdüzü, for example, is planned as 18 blocks around landscaped courtyards with a children's playground, a sports court and a walking track, while Lotus Koru 2 surrounds its low-rise blocks with generous green space and has a public park at its doorstep. When you compare complexes, look beyond the list of facilities and ask how they are managed and maintained, since this shapes daily life as much as the facilities themselves.
## Earthquake-resistant new construction

Earthquake safety has become one of the first questions buyers ask in Istanbul, and it is one reason why many of them favour newer buildings. Buildings designed under the 2018 Turkish Earthquake Code follow the current national standard, and a serious project should be able to show its soil survey report, its building permit and, once completed, its occupancy permit, known as iskan. On our website, the verified project card for Marmara Haven Villa lists these points, including construction to the 2018 code with a soil survey report and certificates. Whatever home you consider, ask to see the documents themselves rather than relying on a brochure, and ask when the building was designed and completed.
## The west of the city: Beylikdüzü and Büyükçekmece

On the European side, the western districts have become a natural choice for many families and investors. Beylikdüzü and Büyükçekmece combine newer neighbourhoods planned with more space, a long coastline on the Sea of Marmara, marinas and parks, and access to the E-5 and TEM motorways, with the Metrobüs line serving Beylikdüzü. Many complexes here are low-rise and green, with sea views from upper floors and terraces. Diamond Marin, a boutique project for only 58 families in Beylikdüzü, is about five minutes from West Istanbul Marina; Lotus Yalı in Büyükçekmece orients its blocks towards the sea; and the villas of Lotus Manzara Güzelce sit moments from Güzelce Marina and the coast. For buyers who prefer the city centre, central districts such as Şişli keep their own appeal, close to business, hospitals and transport.
## Off-plan or ready, and the appeal of home offices

Buyers also weigh off-plan homes against homes that are ready to move in. Buying off-plan lets you choose your unit, floor and view early, and on select projects the payment can be spread through installment plans; Diamond Marin is scheduled for delivery in late 2027 and Lotus Yaşam in late 2028. A ready home lets you see exactly what you are buying, from the finished building to the facilities and the neighbourhood, and move in or rent it out straight away. Lotus Koru 2, Cadde Ispartakule, Lotus Yalı and the Lotus Manzara villas are completed, with units still available. Neither choice is better in itself: it depends on your timing, your budget and how you plan to use the home.

The way people work has changed as well. Home offices, units that can serve as a workplace, a home or both, appeal to entrepreneurs, professionals and investors who want flexibility in a central location. Lotus Şişli, on Piyalepaşa Boulevard and steps from the metro and the Metrobüs, brings together 320 home offices with apartments, penthouses and street-front shops in two towers, and its flex space concept lets owners add extra space to their home only when they need it.

privacy.heroSubtitle: How HADARA Real Estate collects, uses and protects your personal data, and the rights you have over it.

sections.title: Who we are
paragraphs: HADARA Real Estate (registered trade name: HADARA Investment İnşaat Sanayi ve Ticaret A.Ş.; “HADARA”, “we”) is a real estate development and sales company based in Istanbul. We are the data controller for the personal data collected through www.hadararealestate.com (the “Website”).

This policy explains what information we collect, why we collect it, and the rights you have under the Turkish Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK) and, where it applies to you, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

sections.title: Information we collect
paragraphs: We only collect the information you choose to give us, plus the limited technical information needed to run the Website:
items: Contact and request forms: your name, email address, phone number, the projects or topics you are interested in, your budget and preferences (for property and consultancy requests), and your message.

Private video tour bookings: your name, email address, phone number and preferred way of contact, the projects and time you choose, the call app and language, and your local time zone (see section 5).
Resale portal accounts: your name, email address, phone number and country, the listings and photos you submit, and the messages buyers send about your listings.

Advertising source: if you arrive from one of our ads, the campaign details in the link (such as utm_source or gclid) are kept during your visit and added to your message, so that we know which ad brought you.
Technical data: your IP address, browser and device type, and the pages you visit, recorded by our hosting provider and, when enabled, by the measurement tools described below.

sections.title: Anonymous visit statistics
paragraphs: To understand how many people visit the site and which projects interest them, our server records each page view anonymously. For each page we keep only:
items: the page address, without any query parameters;
the site language (English, Arabic, Persian, French or Russian);
where the visit came from — only the name of the referring website (for example google.com) or the previous page on our site, never the full link;
your approximate country and city, estimated by our hosting provider (Vercel) from your connection;
the name of the ad campaign, if you arrived through a link in one of our ads (such as utm_source and utm_campaign), so we know which ad brought visitors;
whether you accepted, declined or did not answer the cookie notice;

the type of device (phone, tablet or computer), its operating system and browser (for example iOS and Safari), the screen size, the time zone set in your browser, and whether the browser reports that it is controlled by automation software — never the device model or any identifier;

how each page was used: how many seconds it was visible, how far down it was scrolled, and the number of seconds in which there was touch, mouse or keyboard activity (never what was typed or where you clicked);

the main buttons you pressed and the forms you started or sent (such as WhatsApp, call, "I'm interested", saving a project, playing a video or enlarging the map), with the project concerned — never anything you typed into a form;
a random session number, and the date and time.
after: The session number is created by your browser and kept in its session storage (sessionStorage), only for the current tab. It is not a cookie, it is not linked to your name or device, and your browser deletes it when you close the tab.
We do not store your IP address or any personal information in these statistics, and we do not use them to identify anyone. Seller account and administration pages are not recorded.

Visit records are deleted automatically after one year (12 months); we use them in aggregate to understand what interests visitors and to improve the site. When a new visit starts, our team receives an internal notification (via Telegram) with the same anonymous details: approximate location, page, language and source. This notification is updated during the visit (the pages opened, in order, roughly how long each was viewed, the number of pages and the visit length), and a separate notification is sent when the visitor opens the contact page or a request form. These details are used, anonymously, to tell real visits from automated ones, and each morning our team receives a summary of the previous day's visits on the same anonymous basis.

sections.title: How your messages reach us
paragraphs: Messages and requests you send through the Website's forms (contact, custom property request and engineering design consultation) are saved directly in our system. Our team receives an internal notification by Telegram and email, and you receive a confirmation email with your request number. Only our team handles them, recording their follow-up status and internal notes in order to serve you. If our system cannot be reached for a technical reason, your email app opens with a prepared message instead, and the information then reaches us only when you send that message yourself. Private video tour bookings are also recorded in our system (see section 5). Messages sent through WhatsApp are subject to WhatsApp's own privacy policy.

When you use "Chat with our team" in the assistant window, your messages and our team's replies are saved in our system, together with the name and contact details you choose to add, the page you wrote from, the Website language, your approximate country and city (never your IP address) and the ad source, if any. Your messages reach our team on Telegram so they can reply, and a secret code for the conversation is kept only in your browser (local storage) so you can see the replies when you come back.

sections.title: Booking a private video tour
paragraphs: When you book a private video tour, your appointment is recorded directly in our system, and we keep only:
items: your name, email address, phone number and preferred way of contact;
the time you chose, the projects and what you would like to see, the app and the tour language;
the site language, your time zone (to show the appointment in your local time) and the advertising source, if any;
the booking reference, date and status.
after: We use this information only to organise the tour and contact you about it: you receive a confirmation email, and our team receives an internal notification (by email and Telegram) with the booking details. Only our management team can see bookings. If our team confirms or changes the time, you receive another email; a new time comes with two buttons to tell us whether it suits you, and your answer is saved with the booking. The day before the tour, you receive a reminder by email.
Each booking is deleted automatically one year after the tour date, and you can ask us to delete it sooner by writing to info@byhadara.com

sections.title: Why we use your information
items: Answer your enquiries and send you the project information, prices and documents you ask for.
Arrange and hold private video tours and visits to our projects.
Prepare offers and guide you through the purchase process when you decide to buy.
Run the resale portal: create your account, review and publish listings, and pass buyers' messages to sellers.
Measure how the Website and our advertising perform, and improve them.
Meet our legal obligations and protect our legal rights.

sections.title: Legal basis
paragraphs: We process your data on the grounds set out in Article 5 of the KVKK (and, where applicable, Article 6 of the GDPR): taking steps at your request before entering into a contract, and performing a contract; complying with our legal obligations; our legitimate interests in running and improving our business, provided they do not override your rights; and your explicit consent where the law requires it, for example for advertising cookies.
We do not sell your personal data, and we do not send you marketing messages you have not asked for.

sections.title: Cookies and similar technologies
paragraphs: The Website stores a few small items in your browser. Except for the session number, they stay on your device and are not sent to us:
items: Your language preference, so that we show the Website in your language on your next visit.
The projects you save with the heart button.
Your chat assistant conversation, your Find My Project answers and your tour booking progress (kept only until you close the browser tab).
The advertising source of your visit (kept only until you close the browser tab).
A random session number, sent only with our anonymous visit statistics (see section 3) and deleted when you close the browser tab.
Your sign-in session, if you use a resale portal account.
Your cookie choice (accept or decline), so that we do not ask you again on every visit.
sections.after: We use Meta Pixel (Facebook and Instagram), Google Analytics and Google Ads to count visits and measure which ads bring enquiries, but only if you choose “Accept” in the cookie notice. These tools may set cookies and collect your IP address and browsing data. If you choose “Decline”, they are not loaded at all. You can change your choice at any time through “Cookie settings” at the bottom of every page, and you can also block or delete cookies in your browser settings. The Website keeps working either way.

sections.title: Who we share your data with
paragraphs: We share personal data only when it is needed, and only the data that is needed:
items: Service providers who run the Website for us: Vercel (hosting, and the approximate location of visits), Supabase (resale portal database and sign-in, messages from the Website's forms, tour bookings, and anonymous visit statistics), Google (fonts, analytics, advertising and YouTube videos) and Meta (WhatsApp and ad measurement). The map on our contact page is provided by OpenStreetMap.

Telegram and email, which deliver internal notifications to our team: new visits (with anonymous details only), new messages and requests, and tour bookings. Confirmation emails to you are sent through the email service Resend.
Project developers, when it is needed to complete your request, for example to reserve a unit or complete a purchase.
In the resale portal: buyers' messages are shared with the owner of the listing, and approved listings are published on the Website.
Public authorities, when the law requires it.

sections.title: International transfers
paragraphs: Some of these service providers store or process data outside Türkiye, for example in the European Union or the United States. Such transfers are carried out in line with the KVKK and, where applicable, the GDPR.

sections.title: How long we keep your data
paragraphs: We keep your data for as long as it is needed to answer your enquiry and serve you, and afterwards for as long as the law requires (for example, for tax and commercial records). You can ask us to delete your data at any time, unless we are required to keep it by law. Anonymous visit records are deleted automatically after one year (12 months). Tour bookings are deleted automatically one year after the tour date. Messages and requests from the Website's forms are deleted automatically two years after they were last updated. Live chat conversations are deleted automatically 90 days after their last message.

sections.title: Security
paragraphs: We use reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect your data, including encrypted connections (HTTPS) and access controls on the resale portal. No transmission over the internet is completely secure, but we work continuously to protect your information.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: Under Article 11 of the KVKK (and the GDPR where it applies), you have the right to:
items: Learn whether your personal data is processed, and request information about it.
Learn the purpose of the processing and whether your data is used for that purpose.
Know the third parties in Türkiye or abroad to whom your data is transferred.
Ask for incomplete or inaccurate data to be corrected.
Ask for your data to be deleted or destroyed.
Ask for these corrections or deletions to be notified to the third parties who received your data.
Object to a result against you that arises solely from the automated analysis of your data.
Claim compensation for damage caused by the unlawful processing of your data.
Withdraw your consent at any time, without affecting processing carried out before.
after: To use these rights, write to us at info@byhadara.com. We will reply as soon as possible, and within 30 days at the latest.
Because our anonymous visit statistics contain nothing that identifies you, they cannot be linked to a specific person.

sections.title: Children
paragraphs: The Website is intended for adults. We do not knowingly collect personal data from anyone under the age of 18.

sections.title: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top of this page shows when it was last changed.
